about.title: About
paragraphs: My interest in AI began during my university years, when I started experimenting with the first LLMs and chatbots that could communicate in natural language and help with programming tasks. At first this steered me towards practical uses of NLP and generative AI; later I became more interested in what happens behind the technology. In Python I worked on machine learning and image processing projects, training models and working with neural networks and computer vision, and alongside them I studied how machine learning, deep learning, algorithms and the underlying mathematics work. In my thesis I studied the practical use of language models and prompting techniques.

I currently work as an AI developer. Besides building LLM-based systems, RAG, embeddings, prompt engineering, fine-tuning, document processing, OCR, AI-based text processing and Python systems, my work also covers classical software engineering and optimization problems. I am particularly interested in integrating AI capabilities into reliable, well-designed software systems, so I want to understand the technologies behind them, not just use them. In the coming years I want to grow towards an AI Engineer / Software Engineer role where I can independently design and build complex AI-based systems while keeping a research and experimental mindset.

For me, AI should not replace engineering thinking but serve as its tool. I use LLMs and vibe-coding-style tools mainly for faster prototyping, learning, experimenting and supporting the development process, while I consider it important to truly understand the code, the architecture and the technologies used. I like to examine a problem from several angles, experiment with different solutions, and then turn the working result into a real software system.

experience.org: Eszterházy Károly Catholic University, IT Development Department
experience.text: Design, development and integration of Python-based systems that use AI, including model training and optimization. Technology areas: LLMs, RAG and embeddings, prompt engineering, fine-tuning, document processing and OCR (Tesseract, AI vision), AI-based text processing, and constraint-based optimization (SAT solving, linear and logical constraints). Experimenting with agent frameworks. Technologies: Python, PostgreSQL, Django.

Supported three practical courses. High-Level Programming Languages I: procedural programming in C# (types, variables, operators, selection and iteration, arrays, lists, dictionaries and records, text file handling, pseudo-random numbers, methods). High-Level Programming Languages II: object-oriented programming in C# (classes, constructors, inheritance, abstract classes, interfaces, LINQ, delegates and lambda expressions, exception handling, generics, GUI programming) and planning and implementing independent projects. Application Development and Project Lab I: agile and classical project methods (Scrum, Kanban), Git-based version control and task tracking, requirement and functional specifications, system plans, UML diagrams, prototyping, testing, documentation and software quality assurance. Technologies: .NET, C#, Git, GitHub, UML, Trello, Markdown.

methodPage.title: Method
methodPage.intro: How an idea becomes a finished project and where the knowledge behind it comes from: the stages, how technologies, languages and projects relate, and how research stays focused.
methodPage.seoTitle: Method: From Idea to Finished Project | Dorina Tóth
methodPage.description: How an idea becomes a finished project: the stages, how technologies, languages and projects relate, and how research stays focused.
methodPage.stagesNote: The flow is not strictly linear: research can send me back to planning or architecture.

stages.name: Idea
stages.text: The origin, inspiration, goal and basic reason for the project. When the idea builds on existing work, the inspiration and its source are recorded and kept separate from the own idea and its goal.

stages.name: Planning
stages.text: What has to be created and what result must be reached: goal, scope, required components, required knowledge and the main development steps.

stages.name: Research
stages.text: Answering the unknown technical questions that matter for the project, and nothing beyond them.

stages.name: Architecture
stages.text: The structure of the system, built on the research results.

stages.name: Implementation plan
stages.text: The main implementation steps and their order.

stages.name: Readiness check
stages.text: Decides whether the idea is ready for real implementation. If not, work returns to research or planning.

stages.name: Implementation
stages.text: Building the project in its own repository, with source code, tests and project-specific documentation.

stages.name: Result
stages.text: The outcome is validated against the goal.

stages.name: Publication
stages.text: Presentable projects are published with a project README; the portfolio shows a curated selection.

methodPage.knowledgeText: A technology node describes a general concept. A language entry documents how the concept is implemented in one language. A project documents how it uses the concept and the implementation. Keeping them apart means a concept is written down once, and project-specific solutions do not leak into the general description.
methodPage.researchText: Research never aims to learn a whole technology. It starts from a concrete project requirement and covers only what the project needs.
researchRules: Start from a concrete project requirement.
Research only the parts of a technology the project needs; do not reproduce its full documentation.
Validate with a prototype or experiment where possible.
End with a decision, recorded in a technology node (general) or in the project documentation (specific).
If a concept matters in several projects, it becomes a technology node; project-specific implementation stays with the project.
Keep the general concept and its per-language implementation separate.
methodPage.readinessIntro: A project moves to implementation only when all of these hold:
readiness: The idea is clear and the problem or goal is defined
The desired result is specified and the scope is acceptable
The research questions that matter are answered
The required technologies are researched and the required language knowledge is identified
The basic architecture is defined and an implementation plan exists
The technical or practical value justifies the implementation
It is not just re-implementing a known example without a proper goal
methodPage.readinessNote: If a criterion is not met, work continues in research or planning.
methodPage.publishText: The portfolio is curated: only presentable, professionally relevant work appears here.
publish: Projects with a project README that gives a concise professional summary: problem and goal, solution, architecture highlights, technologies, how to run it, limitations and future work.
Technology notes and research with standalone value.
Not included: raw research logs, the full story of experiments, personal notes and details that cannot be shared.
